speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I’m Dr. Agent. Can you tell me more about the shooting ear pain and how long it has been since your tympanoplasty? Are you experiencing any discharge or hearing changes?

speaker: Patient
text: 25-year-old female. The patient has a history of polycystic ovarian syndrome, depression, and chronic bilateral ear infections. She underwent right ear tympanoplasty 12 weeks ago. Although audiology report from one week ago showed improved hearing by 20 decibels, she reports occasional shooting pain when eating and discomfort when wearing earrings. She describes her job as stressful and mentions poor sleep quality.

speaker: Doctor
text: I notice you mentioned occasional shooting pain specifically when eating. Does this pain radiate to your jaw or temple, and do you experience any tenderness when I palpate the area in front of your ear?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Occasional shooting pain in the ear with eating. I also have Discomfort when wearing earrings, Stress from job, Poor sleep quality.

speaker: Doctor
text: Does the pain feel like it originates from inside the ear canal or deep within the ear itself, and do you have any numbness or tingling on the front of your earlobe? I am checking for signs of greater auricular nerve involvement or external auditory canal issues.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: History of polycystic ovarian syndrome, depression, and chronic bilateral ear infections. Underwent right ear tympanoplasty 12 weeks prior. Social history: Works as a cashier at a local department store.

speaker: Doctor
text: Let me palpate the tragus and the area just anterior to your ear canal to check for tenderness or swelling, which would suggest external auditory canal inflammation. Do you feel any pain or sensitivity when I gently press on these specific spots?

Does the otoscopic exam reveal any signs of granulation tissue, cholesteatoma recurrence, or inflammation at the tympanoplasty site, particularly near the tragus or earlobe where the earring discomfort is noted?

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the normal otoscopic exam and pain triggered by eating, I suspect this is referred pain from temporomandibular joint dysfunction rather than an ear pathology. Do you experience clicking, popping, or limited movement in your jaw, and is there tenderness when I palpate your temporomandibular joint?

speaker: Doctor
text: Since the ear exam is normal and jaw symptoms are denied, I suspect the pain is neuropathic, possibly involving the auriculotemporal nerve irritated during surgery. I will request an MRI to rule out any structural nerve compression or soft tissue abnormalities in the periauricular region. REQUEST TEST: MRI_Head_and_Neck

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: MRI of the head and neck shows no evidence of structural nerve compression, masses, or soft tissue abnormalities in the periauricular region. The tympanic membrane graft is intact. No signs of cholesteatoma recurrence or active inflammation are present.

speaker: Doctor
text: With normal imaging and otoscopy, I suspect this is occipital neuralgia or a tension-related neuralgia exacerbated by your stress and poor sleep. Do you have tenderness at the base of your skull, and does the pain feel like electric shocks radiating from the back of your head to the ear?
